findings.title: Cache entries are retained when device-limit admission fails
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, but does not remove it when that call returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. The first request from a new device at capacity is rejected, but its ID remains cached for 29 minutes; a retry then exits at the cache hit on line 83 without checking the store and authentication succeeds. This makes the configured device limit bypassable after one failed attempt per device ID.

findings.title: Device-limit check and insertion are not atomic
findings.body: The active-device count is read in one database session and the subsequent insert/upsert is performed later in another session. Multiple requests for distinct devices can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then all insert successfully, exceeding the configured limit. The limit needs to be enforced transactionally/with suitable locking or a database-side admission mechanism; the current count-then-insert sequence is inherently racy under concurrent anonymous requests.

findings.title: Anonymous clients can bypass the limit by omitting the device header
findings.body: Authentication only rejects when `TagDevice` returns the limit error, but `TagDevice` returns success without recording anything when `X-Grafana-Device-Id` is absent. Since this header is entirely supplied by the anonymous client, requests without it are authenticated even after the configured limit has been reached. A device cap intended to restrict anonymous access cannot be enforced through an optional client-controlled identifier.
